title: Phaedria V. Alexander - KOGT
content: The Celebration of Life for Ms. Phaedria V. Alexander, 60, of Orange, will be Wednesday, November 18, 2026, at 11am at Wesley United Methodist Church under the direction of Sparrow Funeral Home. Rites of Christian Burial will follow at Magnolia Memorial Gardens Cemetery. A loving soul to all who knew her.  Phaedria (Phae) Von Astoria Alexander was born  in Orange, TX  December 30, 1965, to Beverly Yvonne (Hall) Alexander and  Franklin George Alexander. Gone too soon, she passed away at Harbor Hospice House in Beaumont, Texas. Raised in Orange, Phae attended West Orange- Stark High School where she was an active clarinet player in the Marching Band.  She gained lifelong friendships before graduating with the Class of 1984. After graduating from Lamar University with an Associate of Science Degree, Phaedria moved to Houston where she spent 30 years working as a mid-level manager. Over the course of her lifetime and at every job in between, Phae met co-workers who became friends who then became sisters and she loved each one of them dearly. Phae was a compassionate sister to all her siblings and loved them with all her heart.  She played both the role of “Lil Sis”  and “BIG Sis,” always checking in to make sure they were all doing well and would lend her help however needed. In the last 5 years of her life, Phae moved back to Orange where she helped care for her stepmother, Mary Alexander, and assumed the role of primary caretaker for her father, George. To cherish her memories Phaedria leaves behind her siblings, Sebastian Alexander (Lara), Tiffany Stout (Brandon), Karl Lynn Lathan, Christopher Lathan, and Naudia Lisa Lathan and a host of nieces and nephews. She was proceeded in death by her parents, Beverly Yvonne  Lathan and Franklin George Alexander, stepparents, Mary E Alexander, and Carl H Lathan, III, siblings, Darnell Lathan and Terhea Lathan,  grandparents, Ethel Mae Walker Davis, and George McClain Alexander,  her great great aunt and uncle,  Bertha B. “Big Momma” Hall and Eddie Hall, and also great great aunt, Maggie B. title: Spain vs England player ratings: Jude Bellingham stars in Three Lions' victory - BBC
content: Ben White scored England's third goal on his first start for the team since March 2022 England went 3-0 up before surviving a late onslaught after going down to 10 men to earn a landmark victory against World Cup holders Spain in Madrid on Sunday night. Here's how we rated the players following the Three Lions' 3-2 victory and you can see how you scored them below. Unai Simon: Made some brilliant saves early in the first half but still conceded three. 7 Marc Pubill: Had a bright 20 minutes against Anthony Gordon until he came off injured. 6 Pau Cubarsi: Gave away the penalty that Harry Kane scored for England's opener. 5 Aymeric Laporte: Always under pressure against Kane but came into the game more as the England striker dropped deeper after the sending off. 7 Marc Cucarella: Tried to get under Morgan Rogers' skin and kept him fairly quiet. 6 Fabian Ruiz: Made little impact in midfield before he came off at half-time. 5 Mikel Merino: The Arsenal midfielder was ineffective and quiet for the first half - and then taken off at half-time. 5 Lamine Yamal: Lewis Hall and Jarell Quansah has to double up to contain him. Moments of brilliance throughout. 8 Alex Baena: The Atletico Madrid forward made some decent runs into the box. 7 Mikel Oyarzabal: Scored Spain's penalty to make it 3-1. Relatively quiet other than that. 7 Pedro Porro (on 20, Pubill): Worked hard against Gordon. Had a great chance against James Trafford. 7 Dean Huijsen (on 46, Cubarsi): Struggled initially against Kane but coped better after Elliot Anderson was sent off. 6 Pedri (on 46, Fabien Ruiz): Constructive and rarely wasted a pass. 8 Fermin Lopez (on 46, Merino) Very good and linked up with Yamal well. 8 Nico Williams (on 71, Zubimendi) Made an immediate impact with a goal and constantly a threat. 8 Subs not used: Barrios, Garcia, Munoz, Pino, Raya, Roca, Torres James Trafford: Had little to do until Quansah's error led to Oyarzabal's successful penalty but made crucial saves in closing stages to see England home. 8 Ben White: That is one way to silence the boo-boys! Marked his first international start since March 2022 with a brilliant all-round display and the eventual winner. 8 Ezri Konsa: Returned to the side after missing Croatia game through injury and proved just how important he has become. Colossal. 8 Jarell Quansah: Was having a good night until making the mistake that led to Spain's opener from the spot and Anderson's red card. 5 Lewis Hall: Growing in stature at international level. Excelled in the attacking third and battled well against Yamal. 8 Elliot Anderson: Utterly brilliant until being shown a red card in trying to clear up Quansah's mess. Desperately unlucky. 8 Declan Rice: Organised and drove the team forward - all while on an early yellow card. Delivered the corner for England's second. 8 Jude Bellingham: In his adopted city, the Real Madrid midfielder swaggered around like he owned the place. Oozed quality. 9 Morgan Rogers: A disciplined display from the Chelsea forward and still created Spain problems in forward areas. 8 Anthony Gordon: A nuisance for Spain in every area of the field but dalliance in possession led to host's second to set up anxious finish. 6 Harry Kane: Won and dispatched England's penalty and Spain could not live with his intelligence at times. Sacrificed following Anderson's red card. 7 Subs not used: Pickford, Steele, Hill, Alexander-Arnold, Gibbs-White, Jobe Bellingham, Eze, Ngumoha. title: Red Brawl New York: Fighting and six red cards mar ‘friendly’ v Club América - The Guardian
content: Game played without veterans and stars on both sides One hallmark of Mauricio Pochettino’s time in international management has been his refusal to embrace the term “friendly”. His preferred branding is “unofficial games”. His spin gained a bit of validity on Saturday, in the New York Red Bulls’ “friendly” against Club América, marred by a mass brawl between the sides that resulted in five red cards and a bevy of beverages thrown from the stands. The game itself was odd for a few reasons. First, the Red Bulls have already been eliminated from MLS’s comically forgiving postseason, which means players (aside from veterans like Emil Forsberg) delayed vacations for a glorified scrimmage. Second, the match was announced on 1 October, at which point it was abundantly clear that the NWSL’s Gotham FC, a tenant of the Red Bulls’ Sports Illustrated Stadium, could host a playoff semi-final on the same weekend. That scheduling snafu, combined with the comically poor state of the pitch, became a serious problem for the NWSL club, who settled for 5,000-seat Icahn Stadium for Sunday’s semi-final. For the Red Bulls, the show must go on – and boy, did they find a way to entertain the fans who showed up for the low-stakes affair. Not with their soccer exploits, mind you. Playing without the aforementioned veterans and US internationals Julian Hall and Adri Mehmeti, the remaining Red Bulls came ready for a scrap. At one point in the second half, América goalkeeper Rodolfo Cota required treatment for taking a boot above his knee while closing a shooting angle, putting the visitors on alert. Roughly 40 minutes into the second half, this unofficial game abandoned any attempt to be friendly. Mijahir Jiménez dribbled toward the right corner flag, only to be taken down by a defender. He took great umbrage to the nature of the challenge, kicking off a maelstrom of shoves, punches, thrown drinks from the crowd, and men pressing their chests and foreheads together like bighorn rams in the throes of the rutting season. The full sequence lives on thanks to a live watch-along streamed on YouTube, where former Mexico defender Miguel Layún comes to life in his gamer chair and begs his compatriots to keep the fracas alive. The fracas lasted 65 seconds, while the ensuing corner kick came a full seven minutes after Jimenez’s dribble. The only scoreline from the night that matters: three Red Bulls sent off, three players from América, with the final five minutes being an eight-v-eight affair. The referee decided to forego any second half stoppage time, almost certainly for the best. The Guardian has something US newsrooms don’t: guaranteed independence. title: The V is for "Victory" - NCPR: North Country Public Radio
content:
As you might have figured out over the years, I am a radio nerd.  So it probably makes sense that I am the manager of a public radio station.  More sense that if I were, say, a leek farmer.  I suppose there’s no reason a leek farmer can’t be a radio nerd, but if there were a good profession for a radio nerd, it is probably “radio.” I wouldn’t call my trip to Newfoundland last week a “radio pilgrimage,” exactly, but it did put me in touch with the roots of my radio nerd-dom. I was five years old when my family flew to Scandinavia for a summer vacation.  I remember two things about that flight: The very end, in which a very small, jean jacketed version of me was lifted off the bottom stair of the gangway by a very blonde flight attendant who exclaimed, “Welcome to Norway!”  But more to the point, I remember looking out the window of the Pan Am 747 partway through the flight, and staring at an otherworldly sight of icebergs and a strange, rocky landscape 30,000 feet below. “That’s Newfoundland,” said the flight attendant.  It was a different flight attendant than the one who hoisted me in the air. And it was not the last time Newfoundland would enter the consciousness of a young Mitch. Not long after that fateful summer, I acquired a pocket-size transistor radio, whose tiny AM dial could pull in radio stations from hundreds - even thousands - of miles away.  And late at night, when I should have been developing good sleeping habits, I would turn the dial, millimeter by millimeter, listening for stations from far away places.  And then I would record them in a journal, where I would jot down the call letters, the location, and any other details that I thought were interesting.  (I told you I was a radio nerd.) And the most distant place that my little radio pulled in was: not Newfoundland.  It was Bonaire, in the Netherlands Antilles, where they apparently had no limits on how many watts a radio station could use.  But my little habit led my parents to get me a couple of books.  One was on the history of radio, in which I learned about the first transatlantic wireless broadcast, in which Guglielmo Marconi successfully received (really) the letter S in Morse Code, sent from Cornwall, England, to his antenna in St. John’s, Newfoundland.  This was immediately followed by six minutes of promos for next week’s broadcasts, which were to include the letter R, and the Morse Code pregame show for the 1902 Rose Bowl. The other was something called “Broadcasters’ Yearbook,” which had details about every radio station in the U.S. and Canada, including their frequency, the names of key staff members, their mailing addresses, and their call letters. And this was the really interesting part for me.  Because from my trundle bed in Maryland, I had already pulled in dozens of stations that started with “W,” the handful of stations east of the Mississippi that started with “K” (KDKA in Pittsburgh and KYW in Philadelphia, say), and even a few “C” stations from Canada.  But there, towards the end of Broadcasters’ Yearbook, was the list of stations in Newfoundland.  And some of them started with... “V.”  (I know! OMG!) So hearing a V station became my radio Holy Grail.  But no matter how incrementally I turned the dial, it was a quest that remained unfulfilled. There aren’t that many radio stations that start with V anymore - it was the letter the island was assigned before it became part of Canada in 1949.  But there are a few.  And if you find yourself at Cape Spear - the easternmost point in North America - early on a Saturday morning, you can turn on your car radio, punch up 800 on the longwave, and find yourself listening to the most delightfully Newfoundland-sounding VOWR. Which I did, and made a note to add it to my radio journal, should it ever resurface. I also made the trip up Signal Hill, where Marconi had communicated with England 125 years ago.  And because - as in 1901 - the hill has excellent reception, I called my daughter in England on WhatsApp.  Just like Marconi.
